```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Fixed seed so the split (and every number below) is reproducible
set.seed(123)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5)

pkgs <- c("pROC", "ggplot2", "stargazer", "data.table")
to_install <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% installed.packages()[, 1]]
if (length(to_install) > 0) install.packages(to_install, quiet = TRUE)
invisible(lapply(pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE))
```

This is the instructor solution to the week 10 mini-project exercise. Your
numbers may differ slightly from the ones below: with the same seed,
different split functions (R's `sample()`, `caTools`, scikit-learn) draw
different random splits. The story should be the same.

# Task 1: Load and explore

```{r load}
df <- fread("../data/ad_click_data.csv")
head(df)
summary(df)

# Baseline click rate: the share of impressions that got a click
mean(df$click)
```

**Which variable is the outcome, and which features are categorical vs. numeric?**

The outcome is **`click`**, coded 0/1. Categorical features: **`device`**,
**`ad_position`**, **`user_segment`** (plus the two 0/1 dummies
**`topic_match`** and **`past_ctr_hi`**). Numeric features:
**`pages_viewed`** and **`time_on_site`**. The baseline click rate is about
**30%**: useful later, because any model has to beat the "predict the base
rate for everyone" benchmark.

# Task 2: Train/test split

```{r split}
train_idx <- sample(nrow(df), size = round(0.7 * nrow(df)))
train <- df[train_idx, ]
test  <- df[-train_idx, ]
```

**Why do we evaluate the model on data it never saw during training?**

Because performance on the training data is **optimistic**: the model has
already seen those rows and can fit their noise. The test set gives an
honest estimate of how the model will do on **new** impressions, which is
the only thing the ad team cares about.

# Task 3: Fit two logits and keep the better one

Our pick: **`past_ctr_hi`** and **`topic_match`**. The logic: one describes
the *user* (do they click ads in general?) and one describes the *ad* (is
it relevant to the page they are reading?). Any pick with a sensible
argument is fine; the comparison below tells you how good yours was.

```{r fit}
logit_pair <- glm(click ~ past_ctr_hi + topic_match,
                  data = train, family = binomial())
logit_full <- glm(click ~ device + ad_position + user_segment +
                    pages_viewed + time_on_site + topic_match + past_ctr_hi,
                  data = train, family = binomial())

stargazer(logit_pair, logit_full, type = "text", no.space = TRUE,
          column.labels = c("Our two picks", "All features"))
```

```{r compare}
p_pair <- predict(logit_pair, newdata = test, type = "response")
p_full <- predict(logit_full, newdata = test, type = "response")

auc_pair <- as.numeric(auc(roc(test$click, p_pair, quiet = TRUE)))
auc_full <- as.numeric(auc(roc(test$click, p_full, quiet = TRUE)))
data.frame(model = c("our two picks", "all features"),
           test_auc = round(c(auc_pair, auc_full), 3))
```

**Which model wins, and by how much? How close did your two picks get?**

The **all-features model wins** (test AUC about **0.80**), so it is "your
model" from here on. Our pick is the best possible pair and still lands
around **0.76**: two well-chosen features carry most of the signal, but the
full model adds a real margin. For reference, the pair from class
(`pages_viewed` + `ad_position`) only reaches about **0.60**, so groups'
Task 3 numbers should range roughly from 0.55 to 0.76 depending on the
pick.

# Task 4: Classify at 0.5 and build the confusion matrix

We use the **all-features model** (the winner from Task 3).

```{r predict}
test$p_hat <- p_full
test$y_hat <- as.integer(test$p_hat >= 0.5)
head(test[, c("click", "p_hat", "y_hat")])
```

```{r metrics}
TP <- sum(test$y_hat == 1 & test$click == 1)
FP <- sum(test$y_hat == 1 & test$click == 0)
FN <- sum(test$y_hat == 0 & test$click == 1)
TN <- sum(test$y_hat == 0 & test$click == 0)
print(paste("TP:", TP, "FP:", FP, "FN:", FN, "TN:", TN))

accuracy  <- (TP + TN) / (TP + FP + FN + TN)
precision <- TP / (TP + FP)
recall    <- TP / (TP + FN)
f1        <- 2 * precision * recall / (precision + recall)
data.frame(Threshold = 0.50,
           Accuracy = round(accuracy, 3), Precision = round(precision, 3),
           Recall = round(recall, 3), F1 = round(f1, 3))
```

**What does the threshold of 0.5 mean in practice?**

We flag an impression (show the ad, in business terms) when the model says
the click probability is at least 50%. There is nothing special about 0.5:
it is just the default, and Task 7 moves it on purpose.

**If the business cares most about "catching all potential clickers", which metric?**

**Recall**: of all the impressions that really end in a click, the share we
flagged. Here recall at 0.5 is about **48%**, so the default cutoff already
misses half the real clickers; precision (about **67%**) says two thirds of
what we flag is a real clicker, against a 33% base rate in the test set.

# Task 5: The ROC curve and the AUC

```{r rocplot}
roc_obj <- roc(response = test$click, predictor = test$p_hat, quiet = TRUE)
ggplot(data.frame(FPR = 1 - roc_obj$specificities,
                  TPR = roc_obj$sensitivities), aes(FPR, TPR)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(title = "ROC curve, all-features model",
       x = "False Positive Rate", y = "True Positive Rate") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

round(as.numeric(auc(roc_obj)), 3)
```

**Why is the diagonal a "random guess" baseline?**

A classifier that ranks impressions at random catches true positives at the
same rate it triggers false positives, so its curve is the 45-degree line.
A curve hugging the diagonal means the model barely separates clickers from
non-clickers.

**What is the maximum possible AUC?**

Max is **1.0** (every clicker ranked above every non-clicker). Our
**0.80** means: pick a random clicker and a random non-clicker, and the
model scores the clicker higher 80% of the time.

# Task 6: Odds ratios, drawn

```{r odds, fig.height=4}
or <- exp(coef(logit_full))
or <- or[names(or) != "(Intercept)"]
or_dt <- data.table(feature = names(or), odds_ratio = as.numeric(or))[order(odds_ratio)]
or_dt[, feature := factor(feature, levels = feature)]
ggplot(or_dt, aes(x = odds_ratio, y = feature)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#990000", width = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(odds_ratio, 2)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Odds ratios (dashed line = no effect)",
       x = "Odds ratio: how the feature multiplies the odds of a click",
       y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)
```

**If the top ad position has an odds ratio of about 2.5, how should we interpret it?**

The **odds** of a click are about **2.5 times higher** for an ad at the top
of the page than at the bottom (the reference level), holding everything
else fixed. The chart tells the story the slides need: past click behavior
and topic match dominate, position and device matter, and `time_on_site`
sits at 1 (no effect).

# Task 7: Pick a threshold for the business goal

The goal: at least **75% precision**, at the **lowest** threshold that
clears it, so recall stays as high as possible.

```{r threshold}
grid <- seq(0.05, 0.95, by = 0.01)
res <- rbindlist(lapply(grid, function(t) {
  pred <- as.integer(test$p_hat >= t)
  tp <- sum(pred == 1 & test$click == 1)
  fp <- sum(pred == 1 & test$click == 0)
  fn <- sum(pred == 0 & test$click == 1)
  tn <- sum(pred == 0 & test$click == 0)
  data.table(threshold = t, flagged = tp + fp,
             precision = ifelse(tp + fp > 0, tp / (tp + fp), NA),
             recall = tp / (tp + fn),
             accuracy = (tp + tn) / length(pred))
}))

# The lowest threshold clearing the 75% precision bar
best <- res[precision >= 0.75][which.min(threshold)]
best[, lapply(.SD, round, 3)]

# The trade-off around it, and at the default cutoff
res[threshold %in% c(0.50, 0.55, 0.60, best$threshold, 0.70, 0.80),
    lapply(.SD, round, 3)]
```

**The answer.** The lowest threshold that clears 75% precision is about
**0.63**: precision **75.5%**, recall **33.5%**, flagging 220 of the 1,500
test impressions. Compared with the 0.5 cutoff we buy about **8 points of
precision** and pay about **14 points of recall**.

**Does accuracy move as much?**

No: accuracy goes from **75.1% to 74.5%**, essentially flat through a
trade-off that completely changes what the ad team would do. With a 33%
click rate, accuracy is propped up by the easy "no click" majority (always
predicting no-click already scores 67%), which is why the business goal is
stated in precision and recall, not accuracy.

# If you finish early

## The best pair of features

```{r bestpair}
feats <- c("device", "ad_position", "user_segment", "pages_viewed",
           "time_on_site", "topic_match", "past_ctr_hi")
pairs <- combn(feats, 2, simplify = FALSE)
pair_auc <- rbindlist(lapply(pairs, function(p) {
  m <- glm(reformulate(p, "click"), data = train, family = binomial())
  pr <- predict(m, newdata = test, type = "response")
  data.table(pair = paste(p, collapse = " + "),
             test_auc = round(as.numeric(auc(roc(test$click, pr, quiet = TRUE))), 3))
}))
pair_auc[order(-test_auc)]
```

The winner is **`past_ctr_hi` + `topic_match`** at about **0.76**, within
0.04 of the full model: the user's click history and the ad's relevance
carry most of the signal. That is exactly the pair we picked in Task 3, so
for us the answer to "did your pick win?" is yes; a group that picked
differently sees here how close it came. Pairs built on `time_on_site` sit
at the bottom, barely above a coin flip.

## A different business goal

```{r othergoal}
# Say the bar is 60% precision instead
res[precision >= 0.60][which.min(threshold)][, lapply(.SD, round, 3)]
```

A 60% bar is already cleared near the default cutoff, with much higher
recall: the stricter the precision requirement, the more clickers you give
up.

```{r budget20}
# Or the budget only allows targeting the top 20% of impressions
cutoff20 <- quantile(test$p_hat, 0.80)
flagged  <- test[p_hat >= cutoff20]
data.table(cutoff    = round(cutoff20, 3),
           flagged   = nrow(flagged),
           precision = round(mean(flagged$click), 3),
           recall    = round(sum(flagged$click) / sum(test$click), 3))
```

A top-20% budget flags **300 of the 1,500** test impressions, which lands
the cutoff at about **0.54**: between the default 0.5 and the 0.63 that the
75% precision goal required. Precision comes out near **69%** and recall
near **42%**. Note what happened: the budget picked the threshold for us,
and that threshold misses the 75% bar. If the ad team insists on both the
budget and the precision goal, something has to give.

## How much money does the model save?

```{r money}
# An impression costs 1 cent; a click is worth 50 cents
everyone <- test[, .(impressions = .N, clicks = sum(click))]
targeted <- test[p_hat >= best$threshold, .(impressions = .N, clicks = sum(click))]
money <- rbind(cbind(policy = "show everyone", everyone),
               cbind(policy = "show above threshold", targeted))
money[, cost := impressions * 1]
money[, revenue := clicks * 50]
money[, profit := revenue - cost]
money[, profit_per_impression := round(profit / impressions, 2)]
money[]
```

With these numbers, showing the ad to **everyone** earns more in total
(clicks are worth 50 times an impression, and a third of impressions
click), but the targeted policy earns far more **per impression**. The
managerial answer: if impressions are unlimited and this cheap, show
everyone; under a limited budget, spend it above the threshold first. A
good group notices that the right policy depends on the economics, not just
the model.
